answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for an account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (sub-resources include databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases, databaseAccounts/mongodbCollections).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group. Example to create a MongoDB API account: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRG --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. This is in the core az CLI (az cosmosdb).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer:
Bicep: resource of type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (api version e.g. '2021-04-15' or later) with properties.kind = 'MongoDB' and appropriate properties. Example snippet: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' properties: { databaseAccountOfferType: 'Standard' kind: 'MongoDB' } }.
Terraform (azurerm): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "myAccount" location = azurerm_resource_group.rg.location resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" enable_automatic_failover = true }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: MongoDB-compatible connection string uses mongodb:// (SRV not always supported). Host looks like <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and the TLS port is 10255. Example: mongodb://<username>:<password>@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@myaccount@ . Username is often formatted as '<dbuser>@<account>' for Cosmos DB; TLS/SSL=true is required.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) is billed by Request Units (RUs) for throughput; you provision RU/s (manual or autoscale) or use serverless on supported accounts. The MongoDB API on Cosmos is RU-based rather than vCore tiers. (There are other Azure managed MongoDB offerings with vCore-style SKUs, but classic DocumentDB/Cosmos uses RUs.)

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: MongoDB API primarily uses MongoDB SCRAM username/password credentials (the account keys / database users). Cosmos DB also has account keys for management. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) token-based authentication is supported for some Cosmos APIs (SQL/Gremlin) but historically not for the MongoDB API; for MongoDB you authenticate with SCRAM credentials (username@account + password). If an environment supports AAD for MongoDB, the driver would need to obtain an AAD access token and use SASL/PLAIN or a supported SASL mechanism, but this is not the common path—use SCRAM credentials. (If you must use AAD, check current docs; my practical fallback is SCRAM.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (e.g., npm package 'mongodb' for Node.js, pymongo/motor for Python). There is no separate MongoDB-API-specific Azure SDK for application-level MongoDB operations; the Azure SDKs are for Cosmos control-plane and management. For MongoDB protocol operations use the official MongoDB driver.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: MongoDB-style vector indexes (as implemented by managed MongoDB providers) expose algorithms like HNSW and IVF (some providers also offer DiskANN). The creation is a normal createIndex call with a vector index spec. Example (MongoDB 7+ style): db.prescriptions.createIndex( { embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', vector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } } ); Adjust algorithm and params per provider. (Provider-specific options like DiskANN may have different parameter names.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: There is no built-in Lucene-style full-text search in Cosmos's MongoDB API historically; use Azure Cognitive Search to index documents from Cosmos DB for full-text/hybrid search, or use application-side hybrid ranking that combines vector nearest-neighbour results from the vector index with keyword hits from Azure Cognitive Search. If the managed MongoDB API supports Atlas-like 'Search' (Lucene) then use that feature; otherwise use Azure Cognitive Search or an application layer that merges results.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Supported wire protocol depends on the account configuration; modern managed MongoDB-compatible accounts may advertise support for up to MongoDB 7.0. However Cosmos DB historically lagged and supported older protocols; assume compatibility with many 4.x/5.x client features but verify the account's advertised wire protocol. Commonly-missing features: some server-side JavaScript, certain admin/diagnostic commands, full replica-set control, and advanced sharding/transactions features may be limited or behave differently. Also some MongoDB aggregation stages or server-side operators may be unsupported or have different performance characteristics.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no full local emulator for the Cosmos DB MongoDB API. For development run an official MongoDB docker image (match the advertised server version, e.g. mongo:7.0) and connect to it on the standard port 27017 (mongodb://localhost:27017). For Cosmos DB-specific behavior there is an Azure Cosmos DB Emulator but it has historically supported only the SQL (Core) API, not the MongoDB API.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams require a replica-set-like topology and MongoDB 3.6+ wire protocol. If the managed service advertises full MongoDB change stream support (MongoDB API on some providers does), you can use them without extra account-level toggles other than correct user privileges. For Cosmos DB specifically, change-stream-like functionality exists as the Change Feed for core/SQL API; MongoDB change streams support has historically been limited or absent—verify on the account. If supported, no special flag beyond appropriate user privileges is normally required.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server (the service-specific MCP server) for data-plane inspection and tools; the general Azure MCP server covers control-plane management (resources) but the 'documentdb' server supplies MongoDB/Cosmos-specific inspection commands (collections, indexes, query plans).

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: The name 'DocumentDB' was the original name of Microsoft's Azure DocumentDB service which later evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. Cosmos DB is the multi-model, globally distributed successor and hosts multiple APIs including a MongoDB-compatible API. This Microsoft DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is distinct from any unrelated open-source project named 'DocumentDB'—they are not the same codebase.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Under the MongoDB API the underlying engine is the managed service's proprietary storage engine (Cosmos DB's engine or the provider's managed engine), not a vanilla mongod process. It implements the MongoDB wire protocol so most MongoDB drivers and application code work unchanged, but certain server-side features, admin commands, and performance characteristics differ. Expect to use standard MongoDB drivers but avoid relying on unsupported server internals or admin commands.

answers.question: What connection string env var and exact DB name should the sample read and use?
answers.answer: Read the MongoDB-compatible connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime. Use the database name sample_healthcare_15 for all sample collections/operations.

answers.question: What vector index definition will this sample create for embeddings?
answers.answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field using the MongoDB createIndex vector syntax. Example: db.prescriptions.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', vector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } }) — tune m/efConstruction per the cluster's documented limits.

answers.question: What exact port and TLS settings will the sample use to connect?
answers.answer: Connect over TLS to port 10255 (mongodb://...:10255) and include ssl=true (or tls=true) in the connection string query options. Example client URI: mongodb://user:pass@host:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb

answers.question: Which client library will the Node.js app use to talk to the service?
answers.answer: Use the official Node.js MongoDB driver (npm install mongodb) to connect to the MongoDB-compatible endpoint. For ODM behavior use a MongoDB-compatible ODM (Mongoose) on Node—(Beanie is a Python ODM; do not mix languages).

answers.question: What MCP command pattern will I use to inspect collections/indexes and query plans?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server profile (default) with commands that map to collection/index inspection. Example pattern: mcp documentdb collections list --profile default --database sample_healthcare_15 and mcp documentdb indexes show --profile default --database sample_healthcare_15 --collection prescriptions. (Exact mcp subcommand names depend on the installed MCP tool; adjust if necessary.)
